title: I Will Maintain My Integrity: Job's Oath
summary: Job swears by the living God, the very God who has denied him justice, that he will not lie and will never concede that his friends are right. He will hold on to his integrity until he dies. The chapter then describes the fate of the wicked: their children fall by the sword, their wealth passes to the righteous, and a storm from the east sweeps them away in the night.
story: The friends have fallen silent. Bildad gave a brief final speech (chapter 25), Zophar has none, and Job answered with a hymn to God's power (chapter 26). Now a new introduction marks a fresh start: Job continued his discourse, literally took up his discourse again, as if what follows stands apart from the dialogue. This chapter is Job's closing statement to the friends. He takes a solemn oath of innocence, the first of two in his final speeches; the second and fuller one comes in chapter 31. Job's integrity was the subject of the wager in heaven in the prologue (1:9-11; 2:3), and his wife urged him to curse God and die while still holding to it (2:9). Here, after all the argument, he declares that he will keep it to the end. After this chapter comes the poem on wisdom (chapter 28) and then Job's final monologue (chapters 29 to 31).
historical:
The oath formula in verse 2, as surely as God lives, was the most solemn way to swear in ancient Israel and its neighbors. A person who swore by God's life called on God to witness the truth of what they said and, by implication, to punish them if they lied. Oaths were used in legal disputes when no other evidence was available, a situation Exodus 22:10-11 describes for disputes over property. Job's case against God and his friends has become exactly that kind of case, and he settles his part of it on oath.

The chapter's setting is the same undated patriarchal world as the rest of the book. The images of the second half draw on the dangers of life in that world: war (the sword), plague, desert storms, and the east wind, a hot, dry wind from the desert that could wither crops and damage houses, often mentioned in the Old Testament as an agent of God's judgment.
cultural:
Several of the chapter's images come from daily life. Silver heaped up like dust and clothing piled up like clay (verse 16) describe the wealth of a rich man, since fine garments were a major form of wealth and a common gift or payment in the ancient world. The righteous will wear them and the innocent will divide the silver (verse 17), the kind of reversal wisdom literature often describes.

The house compared to a moth's cocoon and to a watchman's hut (verse 18) is a picture of flimsiness. Watchmen guarding vineyards or cucumber fields during harvest lived in temporary shelters of branches that were abandoned once the crop was gathered (Isaiah 1:8 uses the same picture). Clapping the hands and hissing (verse 23) were gestures of scorn and horror directed at someone who had fallen into disaster; Lamentations 2:15 describes passers-by clapping their hands and hissing at ruined Jerusalem.
literary: The chapter has two parts that sit uneasily together. Verses 1-6 are a formal oath, stated in the first person and built on the formula as surely as God lives, followed by statements introduced by a Hebrew idiom meaning I swear I will not. Verses 7-12 turn to the wicked and to the friends, whom Job addresses directly (the you of verse 12 is plural). Verses 13-23 are a portrait of the wicked man's fate, very much like the friends' portraits in earlier chapters. Verse 13 almost exactly repeats the closing line of Zophar's second speech (20:29). This similarity has led many scholars to suggest that verses 13-23 are Zophar's missing third speech, displaced from its original position. Others think Job is quoting the friends' teaching back at them, or that he is describing what he wishes would happen to his enemies (verse 7), or that he never denied that God judges the wicked eventually. The traditional text gives all of it to Job.

outline.t: Job's oath: I will maintain my integrity
The wicked man's portion from God

doctrines.note: Job's oath is a paradox. He swears by the life of the God who, he says, has denied him justice. Even in protest he appeals to God as the ultimate witness, which shows that his complaint is a form of faith, not unbelief.

The second half of the chapter affirms that God does bring the wicked to ruin, even if not on the schedule the friends claimed. Whoever speaks these lines, the book does not deny that God judges; it denies that suffering is always a sign of it.

Job refers to the breath of God in his nostrils (verse 3), recalling Genesis 2:7, where God breathed the breath of life into the first man. Job's integrity is the integrity of a creature whose every breath comes from God.

words.note: Tummah, integrity or completeness. It is the key word of the prologue: God points to Job's integrity (2:3), and Job's wife asks whether he still holds to it (2:9). Here Job swears that he will maintain it until he dies (verse 5). The book's central question is whether that integrity is real.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. It describes right conduct and being in the right in a legal sense. Job says he will hold on to his righteousness and never let go (verse 6), like someone gripping an object that others are trying to pull away from him.

Tiqvah, hope. It comes from a root meaning to wait or to stretch toward something, and the same letters also form a word for a cord (Joshua 2:18). In verse 8 Job asks what hope the godless have when God takes their life. The implied answer is none.

Qadim, the east, or the east wind. The hot desert wind from the east was feared for its destructive force. In verse 21 it carries the wicked man away. The same wind brought the locusts on Egypt (Exodus 10:13) and dried the sea for Israel (Exodus 14:21).

christ: Job's oath that he will maintain his integrity until death has a thematic parallel in the life of Jesus. Before the high priest and before Pilate, Jesus did not deny who he was, even though it cost him his life, and 1 Peter 2:22-23 describes him as one who committed no sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found, and who entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. Job swears that his lips will not speak deceit (verse 4); the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom that integrity was complete. The difference is also important. Job's integrity is real but not sinless, and he maintains it by arguing against God. Jesus, perfectly righteous, did not argue his case but trusted his Father, and was vindicated by the resurrection. The connection is not a prediction but a pattern: the righteous sufferer who refuses to lie to escape his suffering.

hard.q: Is Job's refusal to say his friends are right a form of pride?
hard.a: Some readers hear arrogance in Job's oath, and later in the book Elihu will accuse him of justifying himself rather than God (32:2), and God will ask whether Job would discredit his justice to justify himself (40:8). Other readers point out that the book has already told us Job is right about the central point: he did not suffer because of hidden sin, and God himself says so (1:8; 2:3; 42:7). To confess sins he did not commit would have been a lie, and Job refuses to lie even to end his suffering. Many interpreters hold both views together. Job's integrity is genuine and his refusal to accept the friends' false diagnosis is right, but in defending himself he at times speaks as though God were in the wrong, and that is what God challenges at the end. The book does not condemn Job for maintaining his innocence; it corrects him for thinking that his innocence gave him the right to judge God.

questions: Job refuses to confess sins he didn't commit just to make his friends happy or end his suffering. When is it right to hold your ground under pressure, and when does that become stubbornness?
Job swears by the life of the God he is complaining against. What does that suggest about the relationship between lament and faith?
Job says his conscience does not accuse him (verse 6). How reliable is a clear conscience, and what are its limits?
